Agent and contributor instructions for tflspec

Source: AGENTS.md

This repository is the R package tflspec (DESCRIPTION is at the root). tflspec turns Excel and YAML specifications of tables, listings and figures into R programs that use rtfreporter. Its exports start with tfl_.

Where things are

What Where
The code R/ (templates: R/tpl_*.R; the registry: R/tpl_registry.R)
Tests tests/testthat/
Help pages man/ (made by devtools::document(); commit them)
Sample data data/ (adsl, adae, adlb …: fictional)
Vignettes and articles vignettes/
Developer scripts and guides dev/ (not shipped)

Read these first

  • Workflow, checks and rules for a pull request: CONTRIBUTING.md.
  • Adding a template, step by step: dev/adding-a-template.md.
  • The git steps (fork, update main, rebase): the last section of this file.

The three packages

  • Dependencies point one way: rtfreporter <- tflspec <- tflplanner. tflspec knows nothing of tflplanner.
  • The SPEC mirrors rtfreporter’s API and has no shapes of its own. A change of shape starts in rtfreporter.

Pull requests

  • Branch from main and open the pull request against main. (The maintainers work from next; a contributor’s pull request does not.)
  • One change per pull request. Do not stack pull requests: do not branch from an open pull request’s branch.
  • Do not change Version: in DESCRIPTION, NEWS.md or the version line of the AI manuals.
  • When sheet columns, template arguments or the generated code change, tflplanner may need a follow-up (a new column needs a translation there). Say so in the pull request. The maintainers run tflplanner’s tests.
  • Fill in the pull request template. The maintainers add labels and merge.

Record the change in the PR description. A PR never edits NEWS.md, CHANGELOG.md or Version:, and there is no separate memo file. Fill the template’s User-visible change (for NEWS) field without being asked: one or two bullets in NEWS style (what a user can now do, or what is fixed, named by its function or argument), or “none” for an internal change; then “Breaking: no”, or “Breaking: yes” with the migration. The maintainers write NEWS.md from the merged PRs at release. For example:

## User-visible change (for NEWS)

- `tfl_tpl()`'s `ae_pt_freq` takes `min_pct`: a preferred term with less than
  that percent of subjects in every arm is left out (`min_pct_in` says where
  the percent must be met).

Breaking: no

Rules to keep

  • Use fictional data only (Example Pharma, the bundled sample studies). Never put a company’s specifications or data in code, tests, issues or pull requests.
  • R source is ASCII-only. Write other characters as \uXXXX escapes. Non-ASCII is fine in comments and roxygen.
  • Change the code, its tests and its roxygen text together. Run devtools::document() after a roxygen change.
  • Keep the line endings of the files you edit.
  • Split a source file before it passes 2,000 lines.
  • Explain a feature by what it does, not by comparison with another package; name another package only when it is the actual subject (an engine, a dependency, an adapter).

Tests

  • Before a push, run the tests of what you changed and lintr::lint_package(). CONTRIBUTING.md has the commands.
  • Run tests where they are. Never copy them into a temporary folder.
  • Run the tests in one R session too (testthat::test_dir() on the installed package, as CONTRIBUTING.md shows), not only one file at a time: per-file runs miss interference between tests.
  • Point R_USER_CONFIG_DIR, R_USER_DATA_DIR and R_USER_CACHE_DIR at a work folder, never at the user’s own.
  • Use R 4.6.1 or later to develop. The package itself says R (>= 4.1) in DESCRIPTION, so write code that runs on R 4.1.

Git work for a contributor

If you are an agent working for a contributor, you do the git work as well. Their fork is origin; https://github.com/ichirio/tflspec.git is upstream (git remote add upstream <url>, one time only). Check with git remote -v before you start. Run git status first; if the working tree has uncommitted changes, commit them or ask, and never discard them.

Update the fork’s main

Do this before every new piece of work. A fork does not update itself. Keep main pristine: never commit to it.

git checkout main
git fetch upstream
git merge --ff-only upstream/main
git push origin main

Then cut the topic branch: git checkout -b <type>/<issue>-<slug>.

If the fork’s main has gone stale or has its own commits

If git merge --ff-only fails, main has commits upstream does not have. Stop and tell the contributor which commits (git log upstream/main..main). The reset below discards them, so run it only after they agree, and keep the work on a branch first:

git branch my-old-work main
git fetch upstream
git checkout main
git reset --hard upstream/main
git push origin main --force-with-lease

This is the only time main is ever force-pushed.

Rebase a topic branch on upstream/main

Do this when the branch has fallen behind, or when CI or a reviewer asks for it.

git fetch upstream
git checkout <topic-branch>
git rebase upstream/main

If there are conflicts, git stops at each one:

  1. git status lists the conflicted files. Open each one and keep both sides’ intent: upstream’s change and the contributor’s.
  2. If you cannot tell what a side intended, read its commit (git log -p upstream/main -- <file>). If you still cannot tell, run git rebase --abort and ask. Don’t guess.
  3. git add <file>, then git rebase --continue. Repeat until it finishes. Never edit Version: or NEWS.md to settle a conflict; take upstream’s.

Then run the tests of the area you changed again, because a rebase changes the code under them. Only when they pass:

git push --force-with-lease origin <topic-branch>
  • --force-with-lease on the topic branch only: a rebase rewrites its history, so a plain push is refused.
  • Never use plain --force. If --force-with-lease is refused, someone else pushed to the branch: fetch and look at what they pushed before going on.
  • Never force-push main, except for the stale-fork reset above.

When CI or a review asks for a rebase

  • “This branch is out of date” or “has conflicts”: rebase as above and push. The pull request updates by itself; don’t open a new one, and don’t close it.
  • CI failed: read the failed step’s log first. If the failure comes from your change, fix it in a new commit on the branch. Rebase only if upstream has moved past a fix you need.
  • A review asked for changes: add commits on the branch and reply on the pull request. Don’t rewrite history that the reviewer has already read, unless they asked for a rebase or squash.
  • Stop and ask the contributor if a rebase would drop commits you didn’t write, or if conflicts reach beyond the files they changed.
